content: Prazosin is a medication that can be used on its own or in combination with other drugs to manage high blood pressure. It belongs to a class of medications known as alpha-blockers. The way it works is by relaxing the blood vessels, which allows blood to flow more easily throughout the body. Prazosin is available in capsule form and is taken orally. Typically, it is taken two or three times a day at evenly spaced intervals. When taking prazosin for the first time, it is recommended to take it before going to bed. Always follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take prazosin exactly as prescribed, without increasing or decreasing the dose or frequency unless directed by your doctor. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it. While prazosin helps control high blood pressure, it does not cure the condition. Continue taking it even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Prazosin is also used to treat other conditions, such as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), congestive heart failure, pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland), and Raynaud's disease (a condition where the fingers and toes change color in response to temperature changes). Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your specific condition with your doctor. It may also be prescribed for other uses, so ask your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before starting prazosin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to prazosin, alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are currently taking or plan to take. Be sure to mention beta-blockers, medications for erectile dysfunction (such as sildenafil, tadalafil, or vardenafil), and other drugs for high blood pressure. Let your doctor know if you have narcolepsy, a history of prostate cancer, or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking prazosin, contact your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking prazosin. If you need eye surgery during or after your treatment, make sure to tell your doctor that you are currently or have previously taken prazosin. Be aware that prazosin may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing dangerous tasks for 24 hours after your first dose or after a dose increase. Consult your doctor about the safe use of alcohol while taking prazosin, as alcohol can worsen its side effects. Prazosin may also cause dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting when you stand up too quickly from a lying position, especially when starting the medication, increasing the dose, or adding another blood pressure medication. To minimize this risk, rise slowly from bed, resting your feet on the floor for a few minutes before standing. If you experience these symptoms, sit or lie down. These symptoms may also occur if you drink alcohol, stand for long periods, exercise, or are exposed to hot weather. If the symptoms persist, contact your doctor. Follow your doctor’s dietary recommendations, which may include a reduced-sodium diet. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. If you miss two or more doses, consult your doctor. Prazosin may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if you experience weakness, tiredness, headache, or nausea, especially if these symptoms are severe or persistent. Serious side effects include hives, rash, itching, difficulty breathing, fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, or a painful erection lasting for hours. If you experience any of these, contact your doctor immediately. Store prazosin in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of outdated or unneeded medication properly, and consult your pharmacist about the correct disposal method. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the person has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include drowsiness, decreased reflexes, dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for regular blood pressure monitoring to assess your response to prazosin. Inform your doctor and laboratory personnel that you are taking prazosin before undergoing any tests. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
